hints: Start by recalling the test: a scalar needs only magnitude, while a vector like displacement, velocity, force or momentum needs magnitude and direction.
Scan each list for the familiar vectors - acceleration, displacement, force and weight in the first list, and velocity and momentum in other lists.
Check the remaining quantities distance, pressure, temperature, time, density, energy, frequency, power, volume and wavelength to see which list has no direction-dependent quantity left.
walkthrough: Recall the rule: a scalar quantity is fully specified by magnitude and unit, while a vector quantity needs magnitude, unit and direction.
Check the first list: acceleration, displacement, force and weight all have direction, so they are all vectors.
Check the second list: density, energy and frequency are scalars, but velocity is speed in a stated direction and is a vector.
Check the fourth list: power, volume and wavelength are scalars, but momentum $p = mv$ acts in the direction of velocity and is a vector.
Check the third list: distance needs only length, pressure needs only force per area, temperature needs only hotness, and time needs only duration - none needs direction.
Therefore only the third list contains scalars only. This is option C.

options.A: All four are vectors because acceleration, displacement, force and weight each require magnitude and direction.
options.B: Velocity is a vector because it specifies speed in a given direction, so the list is not all scalars.
options.C: Distance, pressure, temperature and time each need only magnitude with a unit, so all four are scalars.
options.D: Momentum is a vector because it has magnitude in the direction of velocity, so the list is not all scalars.
